The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell · November 21, 2026

It feels like this month (and last month..) has been nonstop chaos. PHP2Shell threw a nice little grenade into an already busy month, and while that was happening a GitLab RCE took down Alpine's GitLab instance. It was a whole thing, and as frustrating as it was, I'm kind of proud to say that I got to help respond to the event and write the incident announcement. Ikke did all of the real heavy lifting, but it takes a community to keep a distribution together. Everything, and I mean everything, is kept together by volunteers lending their time and talent with no expectation that there will be a reward for the effort.

We do it because we care for the work being done. Whether it's a critical service enabling a community of tens of thousands to distribute hundreds of petabytes of data that we call "Alpine", or simply enabling a small piece of software to work for personal desires. All of it happens because someone cares enough to do the work. I love this so much, frankly. It's absolutely flabbergasting what we as a community can do with our spare time.

I enjoy giving my time to Alpine Linux, because there's a community, and because we can have an outsized impact on the world by collaborating together. It's not perfect, but it's rewarding. I think I owe my career to it in a sense. I've learned so much by simply raising my hand and being willing to give my time and learn a few new things. But there's a limit to how far you get on donated time, both personally, and as a project.

Not in the sense that it wasn't used; it gets tons of traffic and contains a treasure trove of useful information that people depend on and are excited to contribute to. But between keeping the infrastructure afloat, migrating off of Equinix to new sponsored compute, and mitigating the constant wave of problems, from scale to RCE, that plague a small engineering team trying to serve a massive consumer base, well, it's no wonder that once alice was no longer contributing, the infrastructure languished a bit. This wasn't intentional, nor was it bad. There simply wasn't spare time to contribute to it.

So in November of last year ikke asked if anyone was interested in lending a bit of spare time to fixing that problem. Naturally, I raised my hand, happy to have an opportunity to do so.

This was essentially the sum of information I got about the wiki; it was all that was really documented. And despite my eagerness to jump in immediately and lift it up from whatever state it happened to be in, it took time to get access. We had a release to get out. We were fighting to get 3.23 finished and didn't even get it wrapped up until 12/3/25! So it's no wonder that it took until 1/16/26 before I got access to the server itself to start poking around and even begin to understand how the deployment was handled.

And as you can guess by the fact that I'm writing this post in October of 2026, I did not get in there and immediately upgrade it and move on.

And I think that's important. Even if I'm only giving away a limited amount of time, I hate to rush through things without fully understanding them. There's just no way I can improve something if I don't have a solid grounding. More importantly, I actually really love spelunking inside of old systems other sysadmins have set up. Everyone has a unique flair to how they deploy something. Enterprise admins end up deploying things in a real textbook manner, and when you deal with small businesses it's usually a hodgepodge of "just get it done". I haven't had a ton of opportunities to spelunk FOSS infrastructure though! What I found was interesting in its own right, mostly because I don't think I'd have deployed the service this way.

What ikke told me was spot on: MediaWiki was a git checkout with extensions and skins vendored as submodules inside the repo. You could slot in new modules using composer, and as long as you had an appropriate underlying PHP version to work with, you were golden. But that was then mixed with actual wiki data, like images, all of it lumped together in /var/www. Very simple, but not obvious if you'd not dealt with it before.

When I got into the server, MediaWiki 1.40.0 was running on PHP 8.2 on top of Alpine 3.20, but the LocalSettings.php that controlled the wiki was generated under 1.25.3. Just to give you a sense, 1.40.0 is from July 2023, and 1.25.3 is from October of 2015! It's really neat to get a sense for how long something was tended for. Of course, our friends at the Internet Archive have been archiving the Alpine Wiki since April of 2010, and based on the main page I can tell you we've been using MediaWiki for a solid 16 years now, if not longer. I'm positive it's not the same exact server, but probably the same-ish data. I made notes about all the little important bits I found, everything from extension inventories to known issues and interesting shell snippets I found in the server's history file. Anything can be, and is, helpful when you're spelunking. Truthfully, given the age of the deployment, the public facing nature of the server, and my relative newness to administering MediaWiki servers, I was approaching the problem with the utmost caution.

By the end of February I had MediaWiki figured out, but it wasn't committed until March. And not to bury the lede, but I mean that in the most me way possible. I went through the process of setting up a clone of the staging server in my homelab. From there I worked out how to package MediaWiki itself, and then break out all of the various extensions that comprise the core system into a proper APKBUILD. After packaging it, I was no longer surprised it hadn't been done before. The core extension list alone is absurdly long, and all told we use 36 different extensions for our wiki, so this isn't even a complete list.

And given the complexity, and that this was all production infrastructure, I tried to get it merged into the community repositories before making any sort of change to the production infrastructure. Anything less wasn't really right in my mind.

But it sat, not because it wasn't appreciated, but because we are woefully close to the absolute maximum storage we can host through our CDN. Not that we weren't working on that either; I started looking into our space limitations in earnest in March, when it was a potential blocker to our ability to release 3.24 in June. I knew the package was too big to go into community, but I also didn't think leaving it in testing made sense for production infrastructure. So I turned my focus to the clearer, bigger problem and started working with ikke and clandmeter to figure out a path to archive our older distributions.

By May that problem had turned into discussions with Jason at the Internet Archive, which, as this little aside suggests, was the least stressful component of any of this. Jason is an amazing archivist, and the work the Internet Archive is doing is a massive boon to FOSS projects.

And of course, dear reader, I bet you can guess what happened next. I packaged the ia tool, built a prototype to validate we could actually migrate things, and when a prototype wasn't enough, turned it into its own tool, arkivi, which can do partial migrations and reclaim space while it migrates data. None of that merged quickly either, because, well, we were out of space and had a release to cut. But once again, I had time to donate, and I wasn't going to provide half a solution to a problem I could solve.

This might seem like a bit of a detour, but I swear it's not! We are in fact still talking about upgrading the wiki! I couldn't get the core MediaWiki package merged into a stable repo, let alone any of the extensions, which means it can't be released on a stable branch. As much as I personally trust Alpine and think we do a good job keeping edge decently stable, the reality is that it's a testing area sometimes, and it makes very little sense to run production infrastructure off of it. Or if you are going to do that, you need to ensure you have the time to keep up with the constant churn. You can probably guess my concern here: I might not have that time to give.

There are so many disparate but interconnected problems going on in the background of most FOSS distributions that you just can't fathom until you live with them. And the wild part? Nothing I've described is unique. I work within a community of clever and dedicated people who turn this type of work around on the regular. But as you can imagine, I lost my momentum on actually reviving the wiki too. I got blocked by infrastructure constraints and couldn't complete the task in what I felt was a professional and sustainable manner, so I simply waited. My small problem didn't outweigh the needs of the distribution, and there were bigger problems to solve elsewhere. The wiki was stable, it was fine.

PHP2Shell isn't the kind of thing you leave running on a public server, and the wiki was sitting on PHP 8.2 on a branch that was already out of support. So the wiki went dark. We were forced to throw up a maintenance page and block people's access to the wiki. And of course people asked why, and when to expect it back. Like I said earlier, a lot of people depend on this resource to use our distro!

Which of course kicked off a fever pitch of building, testing, and migrating. I wasn't ready for this! I was missing extensions, I hadn't fully tested the database upgrade process, it wasn't automated, and my packages weren't in a stable repo!

But I wasn't starting from zero either. The core package had been sitting in testing since March. I had a clone of stage in my homelab, and a README full of notes about every odd corner of the old install. The better part of a year that looked like stalling had at least given me some sense of how to proceed.

It would have been nice to take the easy out at this point, but it would have been the most temporary of bandaids:

So it was four upgrades at once: Alpine 3.20 to 3.24 (we're still working on 3.25 at the moment), PHP 8.2 to 8.3, MediaWiki 1.40 to 1.46.2, and the git submodule install to apk packages. Well, there really was no quick fix. Somewhere in that stack something would break, and it would keep creating problems down the line unless the work was done in a way that made it all easier to maintain long term.

Even if I wanted to take the quick path and just get the job done, that's the sort of logic that results in the same sort of languishing. Just run the old stuff, just upgrade the existing thing, keep it all similar, move onto the next thing. Sideload 1.46 the old way, get it up tonight, clean it up "later". I have so little time to give, and so many other important changes that need to be made. For anyone paying attention, that's only getting worse with the literal waterfall of RCEs being announced day after day after day, and we're expected to just keep up with it all. It's a lot, but it will only be worse if we cut corners and stop caring about doing it right. "Later" is exactly how the wiki got here in the first place.

Plus, that's not who I am. No, I'd rather dogfood a new tool I've been working on, finish the packaging work, and prove out that everything can and will work on a v3.24 mock and provide a good stable experience. Anything less would be unprofessional, an affront to the craft, or at the very least to my sense of pride.

Which leaves just one awkward bit. Despite all of my effort, the mediawiki packages are still making their way through testing. The work is never truly finished, there's always one more thing that needs to be done. But I'm confident once everything catches up the path forward is that much easier. Every mediawiki component and extension packaged provides a simpler maintenance path going forward. Nobody needs to remember anything I've described thus far. And anyone who wants to suggest an extension to make the wiki better can actively contribute to that process by packaging and testing it.

It turns out that emergencies are great times to stress test the library coverage of a configuration management tool, especially when you need to spin up a box, test a migration, and repeat it over and over. I could have done all of this with some shell scripts or with Salt, but it's a lot more fun to use scio and figure out how well the little Lua DSL I've put together maps onto things I'd either do by hand or know well enough another way. The reps are the point. Every time something broke, I fixed it in the state, threw the box away, and ran it again from nothing, until a fresh Alpine 3.24 container could become a working wiki without me touching it. If you're curious what that looks like, the full scio state is here.

If I as a contributor only have so much time to give, and my standard is that it's done well and to the best of my abilities, well, then I'll combine pleasure and work and solve two problems in one go. Servers get upgraded, I get a production grade test case for my configuration management system, and the entire thing is held together by spare time and tenacity!

I'll write more about scio in the near future. There's a lot to say, but now's not the time.

Did I mention I try to be meticulous? All of the preflight work isn't nearly enough when working with production infrastructure; I wanted to know exactly what I was touching. So naturally, I wrote a quick diff script to compare stage and prod, and the answer I got in the process was very reassuring. The two servers were nearly identical. The only real difference was prod's exposure layer, with go-away out front and nginx listening behind it. Then I wrote a backup script, because the existing backups weren't something I was willing to bet on. My process was obvious afterward: a throwaway incus container restored from a prod dump first, then stage, and only then prod.

Good thing, too. I could see every place I might trip, and I still managed to stumble.

First up was LocalSettings.php. Remember that file generated back in 2015 under 1.25.3? It had been carried forward through every upgrade since, collecting settings MediaWiki removed years ago ($wgScriptExtension, $wgDBmysql5, $wgUseTeX, $wgShowIPinHeader, $wgSquidServers) and path overrides pointing into a git tree that was about to stop existing. It fell over one dead path at a time. Fix a line, run the update, watch it die on the next one. Eventually I stopped playing whack-a-mole and just started over from scratch. A decade of "it still works, don't touch it", gone. I'll try my best to remember to leave a note for the next sysadmin who comes after me.

Even then, once I could actually open a page on the wiki, every image on it came back with "Error creating thumbnail: File missing." The old backups had never included uploads. The database was covered, but as far as the backups were concerned, every image anyone had ever uploaded to the wiki existed in exactly one place. Nobody was careless here. In the old install the uploads sat right alongside everything else in /var/www, and I hadn't understood where things lived well enough to notice they were missing from the backups. My mock tests never checked for them either. What an obvious and embarrassing look it would have been if I hadn't caught it on staging first!

But then I fucked up. On stage, I ran php maintenance/run.php install instead of update. It was late, it must have been nearing 1am or 2am at this point, and I wasn't fully paying attention. I should have stopped and rested, it could have waited another day, but I had committed to fixing this. If it's not obvious, install is for empty databases. Pointed at a real one, it overwrites an existing db with a fresh schema and admin account right on top of everything that's already there. Thank goodness I had a backup. I was able to easily restore the dump, put things back the way they were, start the whole thing over.

The rest were the kind of thing that just ate time, and they make for a pretty dull story. $wgMainCacheType = CACHE_ACCEL needs php83-pecl-apcu, and opcache doesn't count. The 3.24 mariadb client refuses non-TLS connections by default, so everything needed --skip-ssl initially. The packaged php-fpm listens on a unix socket rather than 127.0.0.1:9000, which I learned by way of 502s. Restored pages rendered stale, because their old page_touched values were older than the freshly built parser cache, which $wgCacheEpoch fixed. And AbuseFilter's grants were redacted in the capture I was working from, so I recovered them from the backup.

When it finally came together, the schema update on stage took 28 seconds. After all of that effort, 28 seconds.

That radio silence was the day job. PHP2Shell didn't just land on Alpine, it landed on everyone, and I spent my days scrambling over the same bug I was fixing for the wiki in the evenings.

By the time I sat down with prod, the hard part was over. It had become routine and easy because I put the learning up front where it belonged. Prod got a maintenance mode, a flag file that nginx checks on every request. Touch it and the world sees a maintenance notice, while requests from the box itself still reach the wiki, so I could test everything from localhost before anyone else could see it. Then the same migrations I'd already run on stage, with no surprises this time. Rsync the uploads into /var/lib/mediawiki/images. Carry over the parts of prod that make it prod: minor tweaks to php-fpm for performance, go-away, the easy stuff.

2026-10-24 02:40:57 durrendal ikke ncopa the production wiki is fully upgraded and back online! 2026-10-24 02:41:12 durrendal https://wiki.alpinelinux.org/wiki/Special:Version 2026-10-24 02:48:22 lotheac nice! 2026-10-24 02:57:20 durrendal thanks :) and it's using packages instead of the old git submodule install too so hopefully this shouldn't languish ever again 2026-10-24 02:57:57 durrendal I just need to open a few MRs now

The wiki is on Alpine 3.24, MediaWiki 1.46.2, and PHP 8.3, and every piece of it comes from apk. Which means the next time a PHP2Shell comes along, the fix is apk upgrade, run.php update, and a php-fpm restart. No submodules or composer, nobody needs to remember something special, all that's needed is a bit of Alpine specific systems administration knowledge and we're golden. This will get better as I finish documenting the new installation, so that when I inevitably run out of spare time, the next person to raise their hand can stand on my shoulders and reach a little higher.

Look, at the start of this I said there's a limit to how far you can get on donated time. I meant that, but not to signal some kind of fundamental flaw in the system. Alice tended to this before me, ikke kept it running alongside everything else, and when it needed someone, someone raised their hand. This time it was me. There are many, many people like me, what I've described is not unique. But look what it took, eleven months from "anyone want to help maintain the wiki?" to an actual upgrade, most of it spent trying to solve other problems around the one that was volunteered for. When the emergency came, it got fixed because someone was willing to pay down the technical debt all at once.

That's what spare time can carry, and it's a lot. It's also why it matters that Alpine is choosing to fund dedicated infrastructure engineering. Not because volunteers can't do the work, but because the work shouldn't depend on whether someone happens to have a free evening when the next CVE drops. Spare time built this wiki, and spare time will keep tending it. It just shouldn't have to hold it together alone.

As for me, I got what I always hope to get from raising my hand, an opportunity to learn. I walked in knowing very little about Mediawiki administration, and while I wouldn't call myself an expert from one small engagement, I'm happy to have come away with a few more packages, more confidence in scio, and a once more working wiki for Alpine. And a great reminder that part of giving your spare time is knowing when to stop, nobody will ever be mad that you ran out of spare time.

#9873. Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:

The GIF below shows the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only shows up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

The student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

#9872. UQ researchers send an unblockable message using gravity

Professor Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Professor Andrew White inside the elevator they used to send a message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland. )

University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter.

The unusual experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between 2 levels, moving its 1.8-tonne counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, ‘Gravity’.

Dr Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics said gravitational communication had an intriguing advantage.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” Dr Woffinden said.

“Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”

Dr Andrew Groszek said the idea came from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge.

“We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr Groszek said.

“Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realised the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”

Professor Andrew White said the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed.

“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White said.

“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector.

“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field from the elevator's movement and translated the message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland.)

Professor Matthew Davis said the UQ team had established an important underlying principle.

“It’s not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely new way of communicating,” Professor Davis said.

“We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

“Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modelling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 metres and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.”

Such sensors could eventually support communication in environments where radio waves, light and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

Read the research published in Science Advances.

UQ Communicationscommunications@uq.edu.au+61 429 056 139

#9871. Build Low-Latency Multilingual Voice Agents: Open Weights & Full Deployment Control with NVIDIA Magpie TTS

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one users notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new)

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

The table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

This release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:

Source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

Latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.

Open weights give developers capabilities that come from owning the deployment. With Magpie you can:

For enterprises building production voice AI, this control over deployment, performance, and customization is often what matters most.

Voice AI in production is a system of models, not a single one. Magpie TTS is part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent Developer Example, a reference implementation showing how purpose-built speech, language, and reasoning models work together as a coordinated system — so you can build always-on voice agents, not just better-sounding speech.

The Nemotron Voice Agent developer example provides an end-to-end reference implementation that developers can clone, customize, and deploy in hours. It includes production patterns for:

Rather than assembling individual components from scratch, developers can start from a complete reference architecture and adapt it to their own applications.

#9869. Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

Give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

We reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

So on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that shows up in the token bill.

Consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

Delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:

On the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

Where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:

Figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

The two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

We give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.)

Both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. Memory is mined from train/dev only; results are single runs (pass@1), as is standard on this benchmark.

The ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

DeepSeek-V3.2 — by difficulty (baseline → +memory): the two systems start from different no-memory baselines (79.8 vs 72.0 TGC overall) because of the prompt-template difference above.

#9867. Introducing OlmoEarth embeddings: Custom embedding exports from OlmoEarth Studio for downstream analysis

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth

OlmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Custom-computed embeddings are now available for users of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

Global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

Computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

Studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

The examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

This query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

The most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

Similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

To test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

From 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates quickly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:

This is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

Sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

Flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

Similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

Custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

While we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's important to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

Sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: The Harness Is the New Operating System

Nov 22, 2026 4 min read

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Manju Rajashekhar, founder and CEO of Mad Labs, opened the conference with the keynote "The Harness Is the New Operating System."

Rajashekhar argued that the harness around an AI model, rather than the model itself, decides what an agent can do and how safely it does it. Each part of a harness, the keynote proposed, maps onto a job that operating systems already perform.

Rajashekhar began with a split that shaped computing history. Applications encoded behavior, while operating systems abstracted the hardware beneath them, and that separation made portable, composable software possible.

AI agents break that arrangement because they generate behavior at runtime. Software therefore needs a new layer that makes that behavior useful, reliable and repeatable, and Rajashekhar called that layer the harness.

In Rajashekhar's framing, model plus harness equals agent, and the harness is "everything in an agent that isn't the model." It supplies the tasks, context, tools, state, permissions, feedback loops and a definition of done.

The simplest agent is a model running in a loop that the harness controls. But "a loop isn't enough. Every iteration has to count," and Rajashekhar described four parts of the loop that make each iteration count.

Context works like virtual memory. The harness assembles what the model needs for its next decision inside the hard limit of the context window, and the advice was to "give the model a pointer, not the whole thing."

The interface works like system calls and "puts a ceiling on the agent's effective capability." Rajashekhar pointed to the SWE-agent paper, in which GPT-4 Turbo resolved 11.0% of SWE-bench Lite issues through a plain shell and 18.0% through an interface designed for agents.

Execution works like processes and permissions. The harness enforces boundaries through isolation and scoped credentials, such as a test database with no production access, because "instructions guide. Boundaries enforce."

Feedback works like return codes. The harness keeps "tests failed," "could not run" and "outcome unknown" apart, so the model does not have to guess what happened.

That matters because errors compound. On a 20-step task with a 95% chance of each step going right, the whole job succeeds 36% of the time, and catching 80% of errors lifts that to 82%.

When an agent goes in circles, Rajashekhar said, most engineers swap the model. A better first step is to keep the model and change the harness.

DeepSeek's model card for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reports the same model scoring from 65.5% to 74.2% on DeepSWE across eight harnesses. The minimal harnesses scored highest, which Rajashekhar read as a sign that more harness is not automatically better.

In a second study, Qwen3.8-27B passed 66.8% of 100 hard LiveCodeBench problems with a single call. Inside a manager-worker scaffold with a shared ledger, it passed 92.4%.

Rajashekhar made a related point on LinkedIn earlier this year. Frontier models are forgiving, the post said, while "open-weight models are less forgiving. They make you think deeply about the harness and how it aligns to the model."

The harness also determines what an agent is allowed to affect. Rajashekhar contrasted an agent that fixes failing tests with one that deletes the tests so they pass, observing that "the difference isn't ability. It's authority."

The example offered was the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI evaluation agents on a capture-the-flag benchmark reached the internet through an open code sandbox. They held admin access on Hugging Face's internal clusters for about two and a half days.

Human approval alone is a weak gate, Rajashekhar argued, citing Anthropic's work on Claude Code auto mode, which InfoQ covered in May. People approve the large majority of permission prompts, and "a tired gatekeeper is a rubber stamp."

The keynote extended a talk Rajashekhar gave at QCon AI Boston 2026. That talk argued that production agents "are just distributed systems in disguise" and proposed the actor model as their runtime.

In the Boston design, each agent task owns its state, receives events through a mailbox, writes each state change to a durable store and runs under a supervisor. The talk closed with a variation on Greenspun's tenth rule, suggesting that any sufficiently complicated agent loop contains half of an actor system.

The San Francisco keynote widened the lens from the runtime to everything the model sees, calls and runs inside. Rajashekhar brings a systems background to that question, having led caching systems on Twitter's early engineering team, which open-sourced twemproxy.

The talk arrives as "harness" has become the common term for everything around the model. Thoughtworks Distinguished Engineer Birgitta Böckeler described it in a February memo as covering "the tooling and practices we can use to keep AI agents in check."

Rajashekhar closed on why a harness design is never finished. Every component "encodes an assumption about what the model can't do," and those assumptions expire as models improve.

Anthropic's harness for long-running apps needed context resets because Claude Sonnet 4.5 showed "context anxiety" near its context limit. That behavior largely disappeared with Opus 4.5, as InfoQ reported in April.

The reverse also holds. LangChain moved checks the model kept skipping into the harness and lifted GPT-5.2-Codex from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 without changing the model.

Rajashekhar asked attendees to open an agent they already use and read its system prompt and tool list. Then, on a task where it struggles, change one part of the loop and rerun what already worked.

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the keynote and can view the keynote abstract and resources here.

#9865. Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

Large language models and other AI systems allow a growing number of ransomware groups to create convincing phishing emails and identify sensitive data quickly.

Ransomware attacks are expanding amid cybercriminals' increasing use of AI tools, but at the same time, fewer organizations are paying ransoms, according to multiple reports released this month.

Globally, organizations are seeing far more ransomware incidents, while the number of attacks targeting US companies has remained fairly steady. In the third quarter of 2026, for example, ransomware groups claimed 2,766 breaches, an increase of nearly 40% over the previous quarter, according to threat data released by cybersecurity services firm Halcyon.

Threat groups adopting AI is likely a major reason for the increase in attacks. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to create convincing social-engineering messaging, find sensitive data quickly, and assist attackers has largely driven the surge in attacks in other nations, says Cynthia Kaiser, senior vice president of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and a former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Cyber Division.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

"We think AI is a big part of [the growth] because it has removed the language barrier for phishing," she says. "We're now seeing much more convincing phishing in Japanese, for example. Countries like Japan are treating this almost as a state of emergency."

Overall, the jump in claimed ransomware cases — up 31% from the first quarter and 39% from the second, according to Halcyon's report — has not necessarily resulted in more ransoms paid out.

Take the retail sector as an example: While 62% of attacks on companies succeeded in encrypting data — up from 48% in 2025 — less than a third (32%) of retailers actually paid to get the data back, nearly half of the 58% that paid in 2025, according to Sophos's "The State of Ransomware in Retail 2026" report.

Instead, a solid majority of retail firms (71%) recovered their data from backup, and most recovered within a week, Sophos found. Other sectors, such as local government and school districts, have seen declines in paying ransomware as well, says Chester Wisniewski, global field chief information security officer (CISO) at Sophos.

"None of them are paying the ransom," he says. "Whether there's extortion involved, whether data theft's involved, it kind of doesn't matter. They're largely not paying the ransom."

The number of ransomware groups claiming success took off in 2026, growing from 75 in the first quarter to 111 in the third, according to Halcyon data. While ransom amounts have continued to decline, the growth in the number of groups continues to pose a threat to companies, Sophos's Wisniewski says.

Related:AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

"There's been five or six new names I've seen in just the last few weeks, so it doesn't seem like ransomware's going away at all," he says. "But its efficacy has been declining as far as generating actual money for the crooks."

The median ransom demand has dropped to $700,000 in 2026, from $2 million in 2024, according to Sophos data.

That hasn't stopped new ransomware groups from continuing to appear. At the end of the quarter, about a third of all claimed ransomware successes came from groups that didn’t exist six months earlier, says Duy-Phuc Pham, a malware researcher at Trellix.

"At the top, The Gentlemen grew from a few dozen victims a year ago to the most active group, ahead of Qilin," he says. "That kind of success makes them the obvious next target for law enforcement, which spent this year going after the shared services these groups depend on, from criminal VPNs to laundering services."

With attackers increasingly using AI, ransomware gangs will continue to broaden their campaigns against more industries in more regions — part of the reason that Europe has witnessed an increase in attacks, while US victims' share of incidents has remained the same or decreased, says Pham. AI allows attackers to create more convincing social-engineering messaging in a variety of languages, removing a significant historical barrier to targeting smaller populations.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

Because of the greater scale that AI enables attackers to hit, ransomware threat actors are able to widen their coverage, he says.

"When a tool can scan, exploit, and move through networks with little human effort, a small crew can do the work of a large one, hit far more victims, and do it faster," Pham says. "That fits what we see on the leak sites: more groups and more newcomers."

The manufacturing sector continues to be the top target of ransomware gangs, because suppliers and partners often share the same platforms, so a single compromise can expose engineering data beyond the targeted company, says Halcyon's Kaiser.

The sector will likely continue to be the top targeted group in 2027, especially as international organizations continue to account for a greater share in the coming year, she says.

"I'd expect continued growth, especially outside the US," Kaiser says. "The big open question is whether more attacks means more money ... countries newly feeling the pain are paying much more attention, which should improve international cooperation."

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).
