#9857. Nightmare mode: simulating disk failures

November 24, 2026 | Anjana Ratnayake, Forward deployed engineer | Teymour Aldridge, Forward deployed engineer

Monthly reliability and distributed systems news, curated for teams building critical software.

Please enable JavaScript in your browser to load and submit this form.

Check your inbox for your confirmation message.

We couldnât submit your form. Please try again later.

Building a correct distributed system is really, really hard. Building a correct distributed system that has to store data and never lose it is even harder.

Many of our customers build systems where storing data reliably is paramount. Storage is hard even when nothing goes wrong. For example, some customers watch how full their disks are and compact data when necessary to reclaim space, and shard it across machines before any one disk hits its limits. Some maintain a write-ahead log so they can recover from a process restart. Others rely on a careful sequence of operations to guarantee durability and atomicity, for example writing a new copy of a file and renaming it over the old one, so that a change happens completely or not at all.

Unfortunately, storage devices are unreliable, which only adds further complexity to every interaction with the disk. Consider a single write. If it fails with an error, the system has to decide whether it is safe to retry or whether it has to give up. If it fails because the disk is out of space, the system may have to trigger compaction before it can continue. Even creating a file can fail because the filesystem has run out of inodes, and the system then has to delete other files to make room.

Moreover, unreliability can come in the form of latency. A disk can be slow, for example because of I/O contention or a failing device, which can then stretch operations out so they overlap in ways they normally wouldnât. If a read and a write end up happening at the same time, the reader may see the old data, the new data, or a random interleaving of the two.

Complexity also arises once you assume the disk will not always be there. If a write succeeds and the machine loses power immediately afterwards, a read after the restart could see all of the data, a random part of it, or none of it.

On the Antithesis Forward Deployed Engineering team, weâve had recurring discussions with customers who build this critical software, and who would like to inject disk faults or storage errors during their Antithesis simulations to mimic these kinds of situations and to ensure their software can handle it. One of the first things we realized is that different customers had vastly different expectations of their storage, and of the guarantees it should provide. This was further complicated by some running on the ext4 filesystem, and some on XFS or ZFS, each with its own behaviors under failure.

This diversity of requirements has made it hard to build a one-size-fits-all solution up front. Instead, we worked with individual customers to build several solutions, geared to their specific use cases. For instance, to test space reclamation logic weâd simulate filling up the whole filesystem.

Other approaches include shouting at the disks.

Once weâd got a sense of the requirements of different customers, we worked to incorporate these pieces of the puzzle into a comprehensive filesystem fault injection mechanism. In this post, weâll give a tour of the disk faults that a ânightmare modeâ fault injector needs to be able to emulate. Weâll start with the fault everyone asks for first, power failure, and explain what it took to emulate it convincingly. From there weâll get into the subtler things a disk can do: torn writes, I/O errors (including the one behind the fsyncgate bug), and the latency faults that shake out concurrency bugs.

Before we get into faults, weâll give some background on how file writes work in the âhappy pathâ case.

When a program writes to a file, the data does not go to disk right away. Instead, it goes into the kernelâs page cache. The kernel then writes it to disk on its own schedule, through a process called writeback. If a program needs the data on disk immediately, it can call fsync, which tells the kernel to write that fileâs data to disk and doesnât return until the write has finished. Data that is written but not fsynced could be destroyed by a power loss.

The diagram below shows these steps for a successful write to disk:

Now letâs start looking at what happens when things go wrong. We started with power loss because it seemed like the fault most of our customers would care about.

Antithesis already has a related fault type, node kills, which randomly SIGKILL a container. The SIGKILL destroys the process, but has no effect on the machine, which keeps running, so the kernel and its page cache carry on as if nothing happened. Every write the process completed still makes its way to disk, fsync or no fsync, courtesy of the kernelâs writeback mechanism. As far as the process is concerned, a SIGKILL is a fairly polite way to die, since you only lose data that the process never handed to the kernel.

The diagram below shows how data that was written but never fsynced survives the SIGKILL and lands on disk anyway:

A power failure is less polite. It loses everything the kernel accepted but hadnât synced yet. Data that has been written but not yet fsynced is simply gone:

Unfortunately, when weâre simulating faults in Antithesis, we canât just pull the plug on the machine. So the next best option was to fake it. That meant dealing with the two things that stop a container kill from causing data or cache loss: the kernelâs page cache, which holds on to unsynced data, and the kernelâs writeback, which saves unsynced data to disk.

The problem was that both of these live inside the kernel, out of our reach. Currently, there is no way to ask the kernel to forget whatâs in its cache, or to stop the kernelâs automatic writeback. However, we found a way around this: LazyFS, an open-source filesystem from INESC TEC and Jepsen.

LazyFS uses FUSE, a Linux feature that lets a userspace program act as a filesystem. Because every read and write goes through LazyFS, it can hold written data in its own internal cache, emulating the kernelâs page cache in user space. Writes to LazyFS stay in the internal cache until the program calls fsync, and only then does LazyFS write it to persistent storage. Also, there is no background writeback to save it in the meantime. This gives us the ability to âforgetâ unsynced data at any convenient moment, simply by clearing the cache. If we do that at the same moment we kill the application, the two together are indistinguishable from a real power loss.

Hereâs a diagram of we can use LazyFS to emulate power loss:

Before settling on FUSE, we looked at a couple of other mechanisms for injecting faults. eBPF was tempting, since it makes some faults, like returning a particular error code from a syscall, easy to implement. However, it would be difficult to emulate power failure, since it only allows us to watch and tweak calls as they go by. It canât hold on to data and release it (or lose it) later, which is the trick we needed. We also thought about using a custom block device, but that had the opposite problem: it can hold data, but it sits at the wrong level of abstraction. Since itâs below the filesystem, it sees blocks rather than syscalls, which makes syscall-level faults hard to implement. Power loss is especially tricky because you canât tell data that arrived through an fsync from data the kernelâs writeback happened to push out. That would cost us the strictness that catches missing fsyncs.

So LazyFS was very useful to us, and we want to extend a thank you to the authors for writing such a high quality tool. We ran a patched version (extended with additional fault types) for a while on a number of customer tenants, and it found some subtle data loss bugs.

After that, we decided to implement our own FUSE filesystem: Amnesia. We wanted to move to Rust for its memory safety, and to rework the design so the model was simpler and faster, since we planned to build a lot more on top of it.

For instance, Amnesia works directly on inodes, whereas LazyFS uses the path for every operation and has to map it back to the inode. Since a path is only a name for a file, this makes operations like renames, hard links, and deleting a file that is still open awkward to track. Working with inodes instead makes that complexity disappear. Amnesia also never touches a real disk. LazyFS writes synced data through to the backing filesystem. Amnesia keeps both the volatile state and the âdurableâ state in memory, which allows us to model an fsync as a bookkeeping update instead of another real I/O. This makes it much faster, and just as safe, because the machine never actually loses power. We made a number of other changes too, which we will get into below.

Beyond the design, LazyFS introduced us to the subtler effects of a real power loss: torn writes and torn sequences of writes, both caused by the fact that the kernel and the disk do not persist data in the order or the units a program might expect.

The LazyFS paper by Ramos et al. is a good read if you want the details.

It also made us aware of the wrinkles of working at the FUSE layer. For instance, the kernel page cache still sits in front of the FUSE filesystem, and it can be holding copies of the data we just âlostâ by emulating a power failure. Thankfully, LazyFS had already worked out the right FUSE settings and patterns to make sure the program never sees them.

Building on FUSE made it easy to add disk I/O errors, another fault type that our customers wanted. The obvious approach is to simply return the error, and that model alone was enough to find some bugs. But because we emulate the kernel page cache, we can sometimes apply the possible side effects of these errors to it, which gives us a higher degree of fidelity.

Out of the box, LazyFS does not simulate disk I/O errors as a form of fault injection, so this was new ground for us. We added the ability to return a few disk I/O error types on syscalls. One of the most interesting ones was EIO (âError: Input/Outputâ, the generic âdisk failedâ error) on fsync.

This error can interact with the kernel page cache in surprising ways. This is exactly whatâs behind the infamous fsyncgate bug. The discovery led to PostgreSQL fixing how it handles a failed fsync (it now crashes and recovers from its log rather than trying again), and it changed how the rest of us read fsyncâs promise for good. As Craig Ringer, the PostgreSQL developer who reported the problem, put it:

When fsync() returns success it means âall writes since the last fsync have hit diskâ but we assume it means âall writes since the last SUCCESSFUL fsync have hit diskâ.

To understand why Craig is correct, we need some background on what happens during an fsync on a typical Linux filesystem such as ext4. The kernelâs page cache holds file data in fixed-size chunks called pages, and marks a page as âdirtyâ when it has been changed but not yet written to disk. When a program calls fsync, the kernel sends each of the fileâs dirty pages to the storage device through a driver. Crucially, the kernel clears a pageâs dirty flag before handing it off. The fsync then waits for the driver to report whether each write succeeded.

Now suppose one of those writes to the device fails. The fsync will then return EIO, but nothing goes back and marks the page dirty again. As far as the kernel is concerned, that page is now clean, so neither the next fsync nor the background writeback will ever try to submit it to the device again. Since there are no dirty pages associated with the file, the next fsync succeeds. Unless the program happens to write the same data again and re-dirties the pages, that data never reaches the disk.

We can emulate this scenario in the FUSE layer. When the fault fires, fsync returns EIO and the affected pages are marked clean in our internal cache, without being written to persistent storage. A retried fsync then succeeds, but the data will be lost at the next emulated power failure unless the program writes it again and calls fsync.

Building on FUSE also let us add âdisk latencyâ, another commonly requested fault type.

Disk latency is really about finding concurrency bugs. Talking to the disk can be slow and unpredictable, and programs that assume otherwise can have races. These races can occur for several reasons. For example, data may land on the disk in an unpredictable order, or land in the kernel page cache in pieces rather than all at once. So we wanted to make those races easier to find.

We currently support two kinds of latency fault:

Completing operations out of order. Instead of answering syscalls in the order they arrive, we let the fuzzer decide the order they complete in.

Since Amnesia sits underneath the program and sees every operation as a request, it can decide whether to answer immediately or hold on to the request. For instance, when data from a write operation arrives, we sometimes hold onto it with a deadline while other operations continue to be processed (the deadline provides a backstop: once it passes, the operation finishes no matter what). The fuzzer then decides when the parked operation should be executed next.

Partially completed operations. Syscalls arenât atomic, and a read racing a write can see the write partially applied. Suppose a program overwrites a few kilobytes of a file while another thread reads the same range. On ext4 the reader can see the old contents, the new contents, or a patchwork of old and new chunks. We let the fuzzer pick which of those the reader gets.

We implemented this in Amnesia by holding a write and splitting it into small chunks. Instead of applying them all, we let the fuzzer decide which chunks are applied immediately and which are held back. Combined with the out-of-order completion above, this means a read that arrives while the write is parked will likely be answered from the partially applied state, so it sees the same mix of old and new data that a real race could produce.

Similarly, reads can be held and split into pieces that are captured at different moments. For instance, a single read can return the start of the file from before a write and the end from after it. With several operations parked on the same file at once, the fuzzer picks the order they finish in. We ensure that every combination it tries is a legal interleaving that the kernel page cache or disk could have produced.

We built our FUSE filesystem to work hand in hand with the Antithesis fault injector and fuzzer. This lets us inject power failures, torn writes and disk I/O errors at moments our fuzzer considers âinterestingâ. It also means disk faults are controlled the same way as our other faults, so we get the benefits of swarm testing along the way.

Unlike our normal node kills fault, which could be interesting at any moment, with power failures we only need to sample one moment from one of the three categories of moments where a power failure can land: before the syscall, during it, or after it. Consider a single disk operation. Within âbeforeâ or âafterâ, the exact timing doesnât matter: if power failure is emulated anywhere in that window it will lead to the same outcome. The interesting states that are uncovered âduringâ an operation are relatively short, so these moments are rare especially in systems that touch the disk infrequently. By tying the fault to the disk operation itself, we let the fuzzer spend less energy finding these vulnerable states and more energy exploring from them.

Our disk fault injector helps the fuzzer by decreasing the uninteresting state space it has to explore. Instead of letting the fuzzer cut the power at arbitrary instants, it makes the decision on each syscall and injects the fault from inside the FUSE filesystem.

Each time the program is in the middle of a disk operation, there are three specific points where the injector may fire a power failure: before any of the operation has been applied to the internal cache, after part of it has been applied, and after all of it has been applied (but before the syscall returns). These three points line up with the three categories above: nothing applied, partly applied, or fully applied. When it does fire a power failure, the FUSE filesystem kills the container, deletes the internal cache, and makes sure any active syscalls are handled correctly. We call these correlated faults, because the timing of each power failure is tied to a specific disk operation.

Our work on disk fault injection has already earned its keep by uncovering a number of bugs in customer software. One open-source bug that we can share is in bbolt, the storage engine behind etcd. We injected all the disk faults in this post while testing the system, but the relevant ones for this particular bug are power failure and error injection.

The issue comes from bbolt committing a transaction in two steps that are each followed by an fsync. First it writes the new data pages, then it writes a single meta page that points at them.

We found a case where the data pages are written successfully, but the fsync of the meta page fails with an EIO. That causes etcd to exit, which is fine.

On restart, bbolt reads the meta page back through the kernel page cache, where the unpersisted meta page still exists, and wrongly treats that transaction as committed. It rebuilds its free page list from that meta page, so the next commits can reuse pages that the on-disk meta page still points to.

Once the cached meta page is evicted, through our emulation of memory pressure or power loss, what remains on disk is an old meta page pointing at overwritten pages. From then on bbolt panics at every open. The etcd nodeâs write-ahead log canât help rebuild the store, because the node never gets past opening it.

This bug could only be found by an I/O error followed by a power failure, which is exactly the kind of problem our disk fault injection finds.

Weâve covered a lot of ground: power failures, torn writes and torn sequences, disk I/O errors (including the one behind fsyncgate), and the latency faults that shake out concurrency bugs. All of these are available in our disk fault injector today, and the list keeps growing as customers tell us what keeps them up at night.

Our disk fault injector is customizable, so you donât have to turn everything on. You can start with the faults that worry you most â power loss for a storage engine, for example, or I/O errors â and add more over time.

If youâre an existing customer, ask your forward deployed engineer to deploy disk faults in your environment. If youâre not, and youâd like to see how your system holds up in nightmare mode, get in touch.

And if thereâs a disk failure youâve been bitten by that we havenât covered, weâd love to hear about it. The best faults in this post came from exactly those conversations :)

#9856. How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?

In our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and showed that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs. the whole set injected — drives both accuracy and cost. This post steps back to the question that comes before it: how much should you give it?

Equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance. It doesn't always work that way. When we scaled the evaluation to eight models — from a 30B dense model to frontier proprietary systems — one finding stood out:

Agentic memory is not a feature you switch on. It's a dose you calibrate to the model.

ALTK-Evolve lets an agent learn from its own past trajectories: distilling reusable guidelines and injecting them back at inference time, with no weight updates and no human annotation.

The right dose differs by model tier: strong models with headroom want the full guideline set, weaker models do best with a compact core plus per-task retrieval, and saturated models show no measurable gain.

Curated retrieval can be both the most accurate and the cheapest option: gpt-oss-120b gained +16.1pp task completion at only +5% tokens — and prompt caching keeps even the full guideline set affordable in production.

Not every model benefits from the same amount of memory. Across eight models spanning the capability spectrum, we saw three recurring patterns:

Strong models with headroom want the full guideline set — every guideline, including rare edge-case lessons. They have the capacity to absorb and apply all of it. DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B MoE) climbed +9.5 percentage points in task completion when given its full self-mined guideline set.

Smaller or weaker models get drowned by a large guideline set. For these, a tight, high-confidence core plus a handful of task-relevant guidelines retrieved per task works best. gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE) gained +16.1pp with this selective approach — while the full guideline set gained less and cost ~50% more tokens.

Already-saturated models show no measurable gain. We call this the saturated pattern — the label describes what we observed, not a proven cause. The model may already have been near its ceiling on these tasks, the guidelines may not have addressed its remaining failures, or it may not have applied the guidance effectively. GLM-5 (745B MoE) sat here in our runs.

What puts a model into one pattern rather than another isn't simply parameter count. Benchmark headroom, context-window size, architecture, guideline quality, and task distribution all appear to shape where a model lands, and separating those factors is ongoing work. The practical takeaway holds either way: the right dose of memory depends on the model, and we can calibrate it.

"Memory" here doesn't mean replaying a past transcript. It means a guideline set — strategies that worked, mistakes to avoid, and edge cases — distilled from the agent's own prior trajectories. The loop is straightforward:

The agent attempts tasks and produces trajectories.

ALTK-Evolve extracts behavioral guidelines from both its successful and unsuccessful runs.

It consolidates those guidelines into a reusable set.

At inference time, the agent receives either the full guideline set or a task-relevant selection of it.

No model weights are updated. The learning loop changes the guidance available to the agent, not the underlying model — which is exactly why it's cheap to adopt and portable across the eight models we tested.

We evaluated on AppWorld — 585 multi-step tasks (168 test_normal + 417 test_challenge) across 9 simulated apps (calendars, messaging, payments, and so on). Tasks are scored two ways: whether the agent fully completes each task (TGC — Task Goal Completion) and whether every variant of a scenario passes (SGC — Scenario Goal Completion, a stricter, all-or-nothing bar). Full definitions are in the appendix.

Because the confusing part of any memory study is what's actually in the context window, we define the configurations up front.

Both memory configurations draw from the same guideline set, mined once (via the loop above) from AppWorld's training split only. What changes between them is only how that one set is delivered — the full guideline set injects all of it every step, while curated retrieval delivers a selected subset — never how the guidelines were produced, and no test-split data ever goes into building it.

The number of guidelines a model mines depends on its own capability, so we report configurations by strategy — "full guideline set" vs. "curated retrieval" — rather than by raw counts, which aren't comparable across models.

Representative models from the eight-model sweep, measured by task completion (TGC) on test_normal:

Figure 1. Representative models in the three observed patterns. Bars show TGC on AppWorld test_normal for baseline vs. the best-memory configuration; the x-axis begins at 40% to make differences visible. TGC alone understates the larger SGC gains — see the SGC columns in the table below.

The figure plots TGC to keep it readable; the table adds the stricter SGC metric, where the gains are often larger:

Reading the SGC column, the stricter metric usually moves more than TGC — DeepSeek's SGC jumps +16.1pp against a +9.5pp TGC gain — because good guidelines especially help an agent clear every variant of a scenario, not just the average case. And the effect doesn't disappear at the top of the range: GPT-5.5 and Opus, both near the ceiling on TGC, still gain +7.2 and +7.1pp SGC respectively. Memory keeps paying off as long as a model has a remaining failure mode to target.

A practical concern: injecting a full guideline set inflates every ReAct step's input, because the guidelines are re-sent each turn. Here's what we observed:

Table 1. Average token use per task, accumulated across agent steps, measured against the no-memory baseline.

Curated retrieval keeps cost near baseline. For weaker models, where selection wins on accuracy, it also wins on cost — the best of both worlds (+16.1pp TGC at only +5% tokens for gpt-oss-120b). Better performance here does not require more inference cost.

Memory doesn't blow up the reasoning loop. DeepSeek runs about the same number of ReAct steps with memory as without (≈18–19 on average), so the added cost is input-token inflation, not longer trajectories.

The real efficiency lever in production is prompt caching: the static portion of the guideline set is identical across steps and can be cached, cutting effective cost substantially. Cache-aware prompt design — keeping the shared guideline-set prefix stable so it stays cacheable — is worth engineering for. We also hypothesize that context-window size plays a role: models with larger windows may absorb the full guideline set more effectively, while smaller-context models benefit more from retrieval that keeps injected content compact. We have not yet run controlled experiments isolating this factor.

The lesson isn't to give an agent everything it has learned. It's to give it the amount of experience it can actually use.

For weak models, that means a compact core plus a few task-specific lessons — which, conveniently, is also the cheapest option.

For strong models with headroom, it means preserving the full guideline set, kept affordable in production via prompt caching.

For saturated models, it means spending no extra context until their remaining failure modes are better understood.

The gains are real across the board — automatic, leakage-free, and requiring no human annotation — but only when the dose fits the model.

This is a starting point, not the finish line:

A learned selector. Our current retrieval ranks guidelines by cosine similarity, which we've shown doesn't perfectly predict which guidelines help a given task. A selector trained on outcome signal is the natural next step.

Memory for very weak models. Below a minimum capability baseline, self-distillation lacks signal. Teacher-distilled memory for very weak models is a separate problem we're exploring.

Beyond AppWorld. These results are validated on AppWorld — a rigorous multi-step benchmark, but a single one. Broader agent benchmarks and real-world deployments are in progress.

Isolating context window. As above, we want controlled experiments that separate context-window size from raw capability.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld tasks are graded by two metrics, both reported as percentages (higher is better):

TGC — Task Goal Completion. The share of individual tasks the agent completes fully and correctly. This is the headline "did it get the job done" number.

SGC — Scenario Goal Completion. A stricter, all-or-nothing metric. Each scenario bundles several variants of the same task (the same request with different data, phrasing, or edge conditions). SGC counts a scenario as passing only if the agent succeeds on every variant. It measures reliability — an agent that solves a task most of the time but fails on one variant scores on TGC but not on SGC.

Really interesting take on agentic memory. The idea that memory needs to be calibrated to the model rather than simply accumulated is especially useful for production systems. Selective retrieval also seems like a practical way to improve reliability without unnecessarily increasing context and inference costs. It makes a strong case for thoughtful custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions, where memory, performance, and cost all need to be designed together. https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-company

#9855. Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

One of the oldest running bug disclosure programs announced it would shorten public disclosure timelines to vendors from 120 days to 30 over the next 14 months.

Google will soon drastically reduce the disclosure deadlines of vulnerabilities prior to publicly disclosing them, and the move has sparked concern among some cybersecurity professionals.

Project Zero, Google's third-party vulnerability remediation program, currently follows what it describes as "90+30" policy: 90 days to remediate a vulnerability and an extra 30-day "soak time" to allow for patch rollout before publicly disclosing the bug. This will no longer be the case. As of the announcement on Nov. 13, Google changed its policy to disclose 90 days after reporting to the vendor. As of Feb. 2, 2027, vulnerabilities will be disclosed after 60 days. As of Jan. 3, 2028, vulnerabilities will be disclosed after 30 days.

In a blog post outlining the decision, Google's Natalie Silvanovich wrote that while the intention of 90+30 was to encourage faster patching while giving vendors time to deliver patches, "The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient."

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

Specifically, Silvanovich noted that large language models have enabled threat actors to find and exploit vulnerabilities much faster in today's AI era.

"A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster," she wrote. "LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior."

Project Zero is not a conventional bug disclosure program. Founded in 2014, the organization was established specifically so Google could help facilitate the safe reporting and disclosure of high-severity, high-impact vulnerabilities found in widely used software and hardware. That said, Project Zero's move reflects a broad inundation of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and where Google goes, the rest of the industry may follow.

As for whether such a thing is good, bad, or necessary for the cybersecurity industry, experts appear to be split.

Disclosure timelines are a key part of the vulnerability ecosystem. When a researcher or firm discovers a vulnerability and submits it to the software developer responsible, a standard timeline is usually designated for the developer to fix the vulnerability; such deadlines are usually 90 or 120 days, but it varies depending on the bug, disclosure policy, and circumstances.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

If the software developer ignores the bug report, is slow to address it, or declines to communicate with the researcher, the researcher may choose to disclose the flaw at the end of the disclosure timeline to inform security teams and practitioners of the looming threat. These timelines hold software vendors accountable and encourage them to maintain secure software, but it's not perfect science.

Oftentimes, the researcher and software developer will work together to coordinate a disclosure date so relevant research, patches, and mitigations are ready at the same time. Sometimes, if the bug is especially dangerous or requires more time to fix, the timeline may change and the technical details and proof-of-concept exploits will be held until a later date.

It's worth noting there are no standard requirements between platforms. HackerOne keeps its default disclosure timeline to 30 days, though it's broadly set at the program level by each vendor customer, and many HackerOne programs set longer timelines. Bugcrowd researchers and vendors generally coordinate timelines; program rules again supersede standards.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

TrendAI's Zero Day Initiative (which is not a platform but a vendor-agnostic vulnerability disclosure program) uses a standard disclosure timeline of 120 days for responsive vendors that release working patches, and shorter timelines for vulnerabilities that result from faulty patches.

It remains to be seen whether the larger industry will follow Project Zero's lead. Dustin Childs, ZDI's head of threat awareness, calls Google's decision "a bold move to be sure, especially considering the explosion of bug reports coming in thanks to AI assisted discovery."

However, he worries about how shorter timelines may impact remediation quality. "I fear it will lead to patches that don’t fully address the vulnerability. We see that happen at 120 days," Childs says. "We’ll be watching closely to see how this change impacts vendors and researchers alike."

Alex Rice, cofounder, CISO, and CTO at HackerOne, tells Dark Reading that he expects the industry to move in Google's direction, though not necessarily in lockstep. He argues that patch soak time no longer protects defenders, given how quickly attackers can exploit flaws now. And because Project Zero is a disclosure program for vulnerabilities with demonstrated impact and not a bug bounty platform that addresses a broad range of flaws, Google is in a unique position to set aggressive expectations.

"The specifics will still vary by program, severity, and whether a fix is realistic, and platforms like ours will need to support that flexibility," Rice says. "But the direction isn’t in question. Organizations should plan for 30 days as the baseline expectation that will shrink even further."

Between stories from this year about AI models capable of discovering zero-day bugs off of human language prompts and vulnerability coordinators fighting huge spikes in bug reporting volumes the past couple of years, Google's position seems defensible. The tech giant isn't alone in its move either: In January, Anthropic's own coordinated disclosure policy will shorten from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity bugs, and 45 days for all other cases.

But not everyone agrees. Expel principal threat researcher Marcus Hutchins took issue with the move in a post to X, where he noted that 2026 has already seen far more CVEs than 2025. "Sure, there are some vendors who just sit on bugs forever and don't make any effort to patch them. But there's way more overworked & underpaid teams, non-profits, and solo projects who are patching bugs as fast as they physically can," he wrote.

Katie Moussouris, CEO of Luta Security and a pioneer in vulnerability disclosure, largely agrees. As she tells Dark Reading, even AI firms currently struggle to patch the issues they find, leaving volunteers and less resourced firms even further back against the wall. "A deadline doesn't magically manifest a fix."

"Researchers and AI companies are burying maintainers in bug reports and not doing enough to help fix them. This isn't even a matter of model access or token cost. The AI companies themselves can't even close the gap," she says. "Anthropic reports that 629 of the 5,087 vulnerabilities it disclosed have been patched. OpenAI's Patch the Planet initiative, run with security engineers from Trail of Bits, has written patches for a third of the 2,055 issues it found, and 23% have been accepted upstream."

[Editor's Note: After publication, a Trail of Bits spokesperson told Dark Reading that of the most recent finding of 2,162 issues found, 733 have a patch written, and among those, 506 (or about 69%) have been accepted or merged upstream.]

A Google spokesperson tells Dark Reading that in creating the new policy, the company solicited feedback from the vendors Project Zero reports the most vulnerabilities to, including open source projects.

"The general consensus was that these timelines are achievable, and most open source projects are almost there," the spokesperson says. "Every vulnerability that Project Zero reported against a volunteer-maintained project in 2026 was fixed in 30 days, except for one, which was fixed in 31 days. Open source projects are among the vendors who will need to make the fewest changes to meet our new policy, as they are already doing so well."

While one side of the argument disagrees with the rollout of shorter timelines, the other side sees it as inevitable or necessary to respond to how attackers now use AI to pursue their goals. HackerOne's Rice says that right now, teams are not ready to deal with a 30-day turnaround, but Google's move may offer an opportunity at the boardroom level to convince technology and executive partners that remediation is a shared responsibility.

"If you're a security team struggling to keep up, don't waste time playing the victim. Take this as a gift," he says. "Ask for dedicated engineering capacity for security fixes, pre-agreed remediation SLAs, automated validation and retesting, and the authority to ship mitigations while the full fix is built. The teams that turn this pressure into that conversation will be far ahead of the ones hoping for external relief."

Casey Ellis, founder of Bugcrowd and The disclose.io Project, says this is a necessary evolution, even if it feels aggressive. In the wake of proliferated vulnerability discovery, the timeline shortening "puts productive pressure on response and fix pipelines."

Ellis says he feels the typical targets of Project Zero researchers are in "decent shape," but community norms tend to follow Google's lead on CVE timelines, so the move could carry larger impact.

"My main concern would be companies that maintain safety-critical systems or those that are otherwise logistically difficult to update; a security fix doesn't always end with a patch, and more often than not, it doesn't," he says. "The Project Zero changes will ultimately reveal (and hopefully shrink or close) the readiness gap for many PSIRT teams, products, and hosted service providers, but unless product vendors become proactive about this aspect of vulnerability discovery and disclosure it is likely to be a bumpy ride for some."

This story was updated on Nov. 18, 2026 at 8:47 a.m. ET, with additional context shared by a Trail of Bits spokesperson regarding figures included in the article.

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

Feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

How you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a new opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date]."

The transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice says never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

If you are leaving due to company changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

Health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:

COBRA: Continues your employer plan for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?"

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the issue your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

#9853. Up to 3.2x Faster Inference with LFM2.5-DSpark

Today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:

The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:

We follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

Under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

We measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

For LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

Running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:

Then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

The block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:

For citations, please use the following reference or BibTeX:

Liquid AI, "LFM2.5-DSpark: Up to 3.2x Faster Inference from H100 to MacBook", Liquid AI Blog, Aug 2026.

#9852. cgo's pointer check is all over the place

cgo does syntactic transformations unaware of Go types, allowing almost unnoticeable changes in source code to turn a 48ns call into a 76µs call. And its correctness checks can panic on legal code, while being exhaustive and expensive in some cases and lax in others.

In this article, we recap some of the basics of Go's Foreign Function Interface (FFI), cgo, and take a look at example programs that explain its behavior and limits. In particular we'll show how passing the same pointer to C can panic on code that the docs allow, how it can be about 1600x slower depending on how the C call is written, and when the cgo argument checker just gives up.Grab dependencies (clang, Go 1.27.0 and Go debugger, delve) and let's get started.sudo apt-get install -y clang curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz export PATH=/usr/local/go/bin:$HOME/go/bin:$PATH export CC=clang go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest Writing C code in Go: how?#cgo provides specific syntax we can use to write C code in Go. It has primitives to write pure C code, include statements, build-time flags, reference C code in Go code, and allows us to call Go code from C as well!Consider this program.package main /* #include #include static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" ) func main() { sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) fmt.Println("sum (calculated by C code in Go):", int(sum)) } main.goLet's walk through each element that cgo introduces:import "C": This is used as a signal to the Go build toolchain that this Go file contains foreign C code. It is not an actual package in Go.Preamble: A special comment block immediately preceding import "C". This is where we can write C code that we want to invoke from Go. It can have two different kinds of content:normal C codeC include statementsC references: We can call C functions and types inside Go code as if they are imported from the C package. e.g. C.add(), C.intWe can build this Go package the same way we would any, using go build.$ go build main.go $ ./main sum (calculated by C code in Go): 7 It works! We were able to successfully invoke the C function add from Go's main function and get the correct output. But it's not clear exactly what role cgo plays. Time to dive deeper!cmd/cgo: the build-time utility#go build first identifies if a Go package has any C code in it. If yes, go build invokes cmd/cgo, a command line tool.cmd/cgo parses the C code out of the Go code, invokes the C compiler a few times to understand what each C reference is, its size and alignment (described in a comment in cgo's source) and finally generates pure Go and C files. Finally, go build takes over, compiles the files and links them into the final binary.Let's look at the file generation step in detail.cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code.For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing showed.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle issues like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird! Let's print out the addresses we're operating on to prove they're really the address of s.small.package main /* #include static void take(void *p) { printf("C got %p\n", p); fflush(stdout); } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} fmt.Printf("s %p\n", s) fmt.Printf("&s.small %p\n", &s.small) C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) fmt.Printf("p %p\n", p) C.take(p) } main.goRunning it, we see both the arguments have the same address:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -5 s 0x2fbb87ede080 &s.small 0x2fbb87ede088 C got 0x2fbb87ede088 p 0x2fbb87ede088 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. Why on earth is the program panicking with the variable and successfully executing when passing the pointer directly?Let's look at the traceback to find out where is the panic coming from:$ go build -o demo main.go $ GOTRACEBACK=system ./demo 2>&1 | sed -n '/^panic:/,/^$/p;/^goroutine 1 /,/^$/p' panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer goroutine 1 gp=0x34af3ed561e0 m=0 mp=0x57d3e0 [running]: panic({0x5629f8?, 0x34af3ee1a030?}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:878 +0x159 fp=0x34af3ed9dd18 sp=0x34af3ed9dc70 pc=0x47b7b9 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer(0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:773 +0x12a fp=0x34af3ed9dd88 sp=0x34af3ed9dd18 pc=0x414eea runtime.cgoCheckArg(0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0?, 0x1, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:750 +0x25c fp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 sp=0x34af3ed9dd88 pc=0x414b1c runtime.cgoCheckPointer({0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028}, {0x0, 0x0}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:626 +0x146 fp=0x34af3ed9de30 sp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 pc=0x47a1c6 main.main.func2(...) /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 main.main() /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 +0x185 fp=0x34af3ed9deb8 sp=0x34af3ed9de30 pc=0x49e785 runtime.main() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 sp=0x34af3ed9deb8 pc=0x44a187 runtime.goexit({}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe8 sp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 pc=0x481341 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. (dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

Grab dependencies (clang, Go 1.27.0 and Go debugger, delve) and let's get started.sudo apt-get install -y clang curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz export PATH=/usr/local/go/bin:$HOME/go/bin:$PATH export CC=clang go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest Writing C code in Go: how?#cgo provides specific syntax we can use to write C code in Go. It has primitives to write pure C code, include statements, build-time flags, reference C code in Go code, and allows us to call Go code from C as well!Consider this program.package main /* #include #include static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" ) func main() { sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) fmt.Println("sum (calculated by C code in Go):", int(sum)) } main.goLet's walk through each element that cgo introduces:import "C": This is used as a signal to the Go build toolchain that this Go file contains foreign C code. It is not an actual package in Go.Preamble: A special comment block immediately preceding import "C". This is where we can write C code that we want to invoke from Go.
